---
title: Plant nutrients and soil
lang: en
free: true
---
Plants require more than light and carbon dioxide to grow. They depend on a suite of mineral nutrients absorbed from the soil through their roots. These inorganic elements become structural components of proteins, nucleic acids, membranes, and enzymes that drive every aspect of plant metabolism. A shortage of even one essential nutrient produces characteristic deficiency symptoms and stunted growth.

## Macronutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium
Nitrogen is needed in the largest quantities and is a core component of amino acids and chlorophyll. Most plants absorb it as nitrate or ammonium ions from the soil. Phosphorus is essential for ATP, nucleic acids, and cell membranes; it is taken up as phosphate ions and is often the limiting nutrient in natural ecosystems. Potassium regulates enzyme activity, controls turgor pressure in guard cells, and helps transport sugars through the phloem. Calcium, magnesium, and sulphur round out the macronutrients, each performing distinct structural or catalytic roles.

## Micronutrients and root absorption
Iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, and chlorine are needed in only trace amounts yet are indispensable. Iron, for example, is required for the synthesis of chlorophyll even though it is not part of the chlorophyll molecule itself. Roots absorb mineral ions against concentration gradients using active transport pumps powered by ATP. Soil pH strongly influences nutrient availability: most nutrients are most accessible in slightly acidic to neutral soils, which is why gardeners often amend soil pH before planting.
